qa.q: Do you read news in newspapers or on the internet?
qa.a: It's usually on the internet actually. I can't really afford or organize a subscription, and it's actually faster that way, I suppose.

qa.q: Do you think the internet is a good way to get news?
qa.a: I suppose if it's simple or factual information about events then yes. But there are a lot of opinion pieces out there that I don't like.

qa.q: Which do you prefer, reading magazines or newspapers?
qa.a: I suppose if I have to choose one, it's probably going to be reading newspapers. I find magazines to be a bit frivolous most of the time.
Online, probably once a day. And then offline, usually when I'm at home. My parents and I like doing the crosswords and making fun of some of the court reports in the local paper.

qa.q: How old were you when you started reading newspapers?
qa.a: Probably before I was born actually. My parents are both journalists, so reading and writing is sort of in my blood. I guess if you want a more serious answer, it's probably when I was six or seven or eight. My dad used to bring home the paper every day, so we'd just read it normally.

qa.q: Do you think it's important to read newspapers?
qa.a: In print form, probably not so much these days when you can get all the information you need online whenever you want it. Although on the other hand, if you read the paper once a day, it might be good for just preventing information overload, to be honest.

I guess by advertising and appealing to tradition in the main. Maybe there are some services that they offer for younger people, but it seems to be usually like older or more traditional people that they try to get the attention of.

qa.q: What effect do newspapers have on society?
qa.a: In some places where communication infrastructure isn't so well developed, it might be crucial for information sharing. And so without them, civil society couldn't really function. More broadly, they're a big part of opinion formation on the issues of the day.
Yeah, you've got to know what's going on. It's important to be well-informed. But if I read more than once a day, I'd probably get depression from all the bad things that people report on.

qa.q: How often do you read the news?
qa.a: Just once a day, otherwise it's probably not going to have a good effect on my mental health.

qa.q: Do you prefer to read local or international news?
qa.a: I guess they're bound up together since Russia and the UK are major countries, so anything that happens on the local level there usually has some impact internationally.

qa.q: Rory, do you discuss the news with your friends?
qa.a: Sometimes. Although I think it's better to avoid it, since my take on things is usually very different to my friends, and I don't really like arguing with people. So, maybe we just discuss the facts and then move on from there to talk about something more personal or interesting.

qa.q: In Scotland, do people still buy like hard copies?
qa.a: Yeah. Not as much as they used to, but it's kind of like a dying media these days. But they do, and there are some local newspapers, although the readership is like getting smaller and smaller by the year, which is sad in some ways, but we're just making this switch to online, and it's probably better for the environment in the long run, I guess.

qa.q: When was the last time you actually bought a magazine or a newspaper?
qa.a: I can't remember. I suppose the last time I bought a magazine must have been when I was back home. I used to buy it when I traveled to Glasgow to see my friend. And then for newspapers, I can't remember. Because, well, my parents were journalists, so they got the newspaper for free.
